subject: mathematics
question_text: Show that the determinant with rows (a−b−c, 2a, 2a), (2b, b−c−a, 2b) and (2c, 2c, c−a−b) is equal to (a+b+c)³.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.24 — LAQ chapter 3 Matrices, answer 15, on a ★★★ SSP (Super Scoring Page), the book's self-declared 'No.3 in Dets'. Printed appearance: AP 18 only. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed against this question, and the 2+1+2+1+1 above is inferred from the split the same book DOES print for the structurally identical answer 17 on book p.26 (1+1+1+2+1+1). It is deliberately the same split this book's answer 14 is given on the facing half of the page, because the two proofs are the same proof with rows and columns exchanged. Star rank is the CHAPTER's ★★★, not this question's. Paper position: Maths-1A Section C runs Q18-Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to the "Column operations C₂−C₁ and C₃−C₁" step.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — say which rows or columns you add together first, what comes out common, and how the determinant finishes.

steps.label: Write the determinant
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own. Add the three entries of any COLUMN in your head: a−b−c + 2b + 2c = a+b+c. The columns sum to the same thing, so the first move works down the columns into a row.
steps.memory_tip: Add the three entries of any COLUMN in your head: they all come to a+b+c. That decides the first move.

recall.must_convey: That the working starts from the given determinant. Naming it is full credit.

steps.why: The answer is a power of (a+b+c) while no single entry contains it. That mismatch always means something has to be added together first.
common_mistakes: Expanding directly, which produces a page of terms.
Assuming the method must match the last question's; here it is rows where that one was columns.

steps.label: Add all three rows into R₁
steps.margin_note: Two of the eight marks, and the whole idea. Down each column the entries cancel to a+b+c: for column 1 that is (a−b−c) + 2b + 2c. Do the arithmetic once and the rest is routine.
steps.memory_tip: Down each column the entries collapse to a+b+c — for column 1 that is (a−b−c) + 2b + 2c.
lines: Columns 2 and 3 give a+b+c in the same way:

recall.must_convey: That rows 2 and 3 are added into row 1, and that this makes all three entries of row 1 equal to a+b+c.

steps.why: Adding other rows into one row never changes a determinant's value. It earns its place when it makes a whole row identical, because an identical row can be taken out as a common factor.
common_mistakes: Adding columns instead of rows — here it is the rows that sum to a common value.
Getting the cancellation wrong: in column 1 the −b and −c are cancelled by 2b and 2c, leaving +b and +c.
Writing 2(a+b+c); unlike the previous question, there is no 2 here.

steps.label: Take (a+b+c) common
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Row 1 is now (a+b+c) three times over, so that factor comes out and the row becomes 1, 1, 1.
steps.memory_tip: Row 1 is now (a+b+c) three times over, so it comes out and the row becomes 1, 1, 1.

recall.must_convey: That (a+b+c) is taken common out of row 1, leaving 1, 1, 1 in that row.
accept: take a plus b plus c common from the first row leaving ones

take a plus b plus c out in front and the row is all ones

steps.why: This is the first of the three (a+b+c) factors in the answer. The other two come out of the determinant that is left.
common_mistakes: Taking the factor out of a column instead of the row.
Cubing it here; it comes out once.

steps.label: Do C₂−C₁ and C₃−C₁
steps.margin_note: Three marks. Row 1 is all 1s now, so subtracting column 1 clears it. Watch the signs: both surviving entries come out NEGATIVE, and the two minus signs cancel at the end.
steps.memory_tip: Row 1 is all 1s, so subtracting column 1 clears it. Both surviving entries come out NEGATIVE.
lines: C₂ → C₂ − C₁ and C₃ → C₃ − C₁:

recall.must_convey: That column 1 is subtracted from columns 2 and 3, leaving 1, 0, 0 on top and minus (a+b+c) on the diagonal.

steps.why: The minus signs are the trap in this question. Two of them appear, and because they multiply together the answer comes out positive — but only if you write both of them down.
common_mistakes: Writing +(a+b+c) on the diagonal and reaching the right answer by luck.
Doing C₁ − C₂ instead of C₂ − C₁.
Missing that the off-diagonal entries cancel to zero.

steps.label: Expand along the first row
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. The top row is 1, 0, 0 so only one term survives, and its minor has zeros off the diagonal — its value is the product of the two diagonal entries.
steps.memory_tip: The top row is 1, 0, 0, so one term survives, and its minor has zeros off the diagonal.

recall.must_convey: That expanding along the first row leaves one term, whose 2×2 minor is minus (a+b+c) times minus (a+b+c) — and that the two minus signs cancel to give a positive square.

steps.why: A negative times a negative is a positive. That single fact is why the answer is +(a+b+c)³ and not −(a+b+c)³, and it is worth writing down rather than assuming.
common_mistakes: Losing one minus sign and finishing with a negative answer.
Expanding along a row or column with no zeros.

steps.label: State the result
steps.margin_note: Last mark. One factor of (a+b+c) came out of the row, two more came from the diagonal — three in all, and no 2 anywhere in this question.
steps.memory_tip: One factor came from the row and two from the diagonal — three in all, and no 2 anywhere here.

steps.why: Counting where each (a+b+c) came from is the check. If you can only account for two, a diagonal entry went missing.
common_mistakes: Writing 2(a+b+c)³ by copying the previous question's answer.
Writing (a+b+c)² by forgetting the factor that came out of the row.
